mainTopic: The אגדה of the destruction and גבריאל's punishment, then the sources that bathing, wearing shoes, and marital relations count as עינוי on יום כיפור
overview: This amud opens with אגדה. It finishes the list of sins יחזקאל saw in the בית המקדש, including men who turned their backs to the היכל in open contempt. הקב״ה decrees fire on ירושלים, and גבריאל is punished for changing how he carried out the mission and for reporting the destruction. Yet the cooling of the coals during the handoff is what let the Jewish people survive. דוביאל, the angel of Persia, takes גבריאל's place and gets a tax decree written against Israel and the רבנן. גבריאל wins his way back by praising דניאל, but דוביאל swallows the decree, so in Persia only some people pay the tax. The גמרא then returns to the halacha of יום כיפור and looks for פסוקים showing that each holding-back counts as עינוי. Bathing is proven from 'מים קרים על נפש עיפה'. After two proofs are rejected, not wearing shoes is proven from ירמיהו's 'מנעי רגלך מיחף'. Finally, holding back from תשמיש המטה is learned from לבן's words 'אם תענה את בנותי'.

steps.title: The sun-worshippers at the entrance of the Sanctuary
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes quoting the פסוק about the 'image of jealousy' and then quotes the פסוק about twenty-five men in the inner courtyard who turned their backs to the היכל and bowed east to the sun.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'There was the seat of the image of jealousy, which provokes jealousy.' 'And he brought me into the inner court of the House of God. Behold, at the entrance of the Sanctuary of God, between the porch and the altar, were about twenty-five men. Their backs were toward the Sanctuary of God and their faces toward the east, and they were bowing eastward to the sun.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting the פסוקים in יחזקאל that describe the terrible sins done in the בית המקדש. These sins are the background for the punishment that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These פסוקים list the crimes that led to the destruction. The detail that matters most is that the men stood with their backs to the היכל and their faces to the east. The very next step will ask why the פסוק needs to say both.

keyTerms.meaning: The 'image of jealousy', an idol placed in the Temple area
The Sanctuary building of the בית המקדש
The porch/entrance hall in front of the היכל

phrases.english: there was the seat of the image of jealousy, which provokes jealousy
phrases.notes: End of יחזקאל 8:3, continuing from the previous daf

phrases.aramaic: ״וַיָּבֵא אוֹתִי אֶל חֲצַר בֵּית ה׳ הַפְּנִימִית
phrases.english: And he brought me into the inner court of the House of God
and behold, at the entrance of the Sanctuary of God
between the porch and the altar
were about twenty-five men
their backs toward the Sanctuary of God
and their faces toward the east
and they were bowing eastward to the sun.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַיָּבֵא אוֹתִי אֶל חֲצַר בֵּית ה׳ הַפְּנִימִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of sins from the previous daf
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק describes twenty-five men in the inner courtyard, backs to the היכל, bowing east to the sun.

steps.title: Why does the verse mention their backs?
steps.stepSummary: If their faces were toward the east, their backs were obviously toward the היכל, which is in the west. So why does the פסוק say it separately?
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the verse says 'and their faces toward the east,' don't I already know that their backs were toward the Sanctuary of God?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that one phrase in the פסוק seems extra. This sets up a דרשה in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The היכל stood at the western end of the בית המקדש. Anyone facing east automatically had his back to it. Since the תורה does not waste words, the extra phrase must be teaching something new.

keyTerms.meaning: From the implication of what is said; signals that one phrase already implies another
Do I not know?; points out that something is already obvious

steps.confusionAlert: This question is not attacking the פסוק. It is a standard way of showing that a phrase looks extra, so that the next step can explain what it comes to teach.

phrases.english: From the implication of what is stated, 'and their faces toward the east,'

phrases.aramaic: אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁאֲחוֹרֵיהֶם אֶל הֵיכַל ה׳?
phrases.english: do I not know that their backs were toward the Sanctuary of God?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Analyzes a phrase in the פסוק just quoted
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does the seemingly extra phrase 'their backs toward the היכל' add?

steps.title: They showed open contempt toward the Sanctuary
steps.stepSummary: The extra phrase teaches that they uncovered themselves and relieved themselves facing the היכל. The פסוק describes this disgraceful act politely.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, why does the verse say 'their backs toward the Sanctuary of God'? It teaches that they would uncover themselves and relieve themselves downward, toward the Sanctuary.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The 'extra' words describe an extra level of disgrace.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Backs toward the היכל' is a polite way of describing a disgusting act of contempt toward the שכינה. So the sin was not only worshipping the sun. They also openly insulted the בית המקדש.

keyTerms.meaning: What does the verse come to teach?

steps.whatToRemember: Facing east already means having your back to the היכל. So the extra words teach a deliberate act of disgrace toward the שכינה.

phrases.english: Rather, what does the verse teach by saying
'their backs toward the Sanctuary of God'?
It teaches that they would uncover themselves
and relieve themselves downward
phrases.notes: They were doing this toward the Sanctuary; the words are just a polite way of putting it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the extra phrase
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra phrase teaches that they relieved themselves toward the היכל as an act of contempt.

steps.title: God tells מיכאל that his nation sinned
steps.stepSummary: הקב״ה tells מיכאל, the angel of the Jewish people, that they have sinned. מיכאל asks that the good people among them be enough to save them. הקב״ה says He will burn the good ones too.
steps.simpleTranslation: הקדוש ברוך הוא said to מיכאל: 'מיכאל! Your nation has sinned.' מיכאל said before Him: 'רבונו של עולם, let the good people among them be enough to save them!' He answered: 'I will burn them, and the good ones among them too.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves from the sins to the heavenly judgment. מיכאל pleads for the Jewish people, and his plea is turned down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מיכאל argues that the merit of the righteous should protect the whole nation. הקב״ה refuses and includes the good people in the decree. The reason, as the classic understanding explains, is that they did not rebuke the wicked.

keyTerms.meaning: The angel who stands up for the Jewish people
Let the good among them be enough to save them

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמִיכָאֵל:
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Michael:
Michael! Your nation has sinned.
He said before Him: Master of the Universe,
let the good among them be enough!
phrases.notes: Let their merit save the nation

phrases.english: He said to him: I will burn them
and the good among them too,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמִיכָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from describing the sins to the heavenly judgment
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The decree of burning includes even the good people of that generation.

steps.title: גבריאל is sent with coals of fire
steps.stepSummary: Right away, 'the man clothed in linen' (גבריאל) is told to take coals from between the כרובים and throw them on the city. But the כרוב takes the coals and hands them to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Immediately: 'He said to the man clothed in linen: Go in between the wheels, beneath the cherub, fill your hands with coals of fire from between the cherubs, and throw them on the city. And he went in before my eyes.' Immediately: 'And the cherub stretched out his hand from between the cherubs to the fire that was between the cherubs. He took some and put it into the hands of the one clothed in linen, who took it and went out.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes two פסוקים showing the decree being carried out. This sets up the next step, which points out a change in how it happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: גבריאל was told to take the coals himself. In the second פסוק, the כרוב hands them to him instead. This small difference is the key to the next two steps.

keyTerms.meaning: The one clothed in linen; understood as גבריאל
The wheels of the heavenly chariot

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the difference. גבריאל was told to take the coals himself, but the כרוב passed them to him. Everything that follows depends on this change.

phrases.english: Immediately: 'And He spoke to the man clothed in linen'
and said: Go in between the wheels
beneath the cherub
and fill your hands with coals of fire
from between the cherubs
and throw them on the city. And he went in before my eyes.'
Immediately: 'And the cherub stretched out his hand'
from between the cherubs
to the fire that was between the cherubs

phrases.aramaic: וַיִּשָּׂא וַיִּתֵּן אֶל חׇפְנֵי לְבוּשׁ הַבַּדִּים
phrases.english: and took some and put it into the hands of the one clothed in linen
who took it and went out.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the decree from the previous step being carried out
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גבריאל was told to take the coals himself, but the כרוב handed them to him.

steps.title: The cooled coals saved the Jewish people
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון חסידא teaches that the coals cooled while passing from the כרוב's hand to גבריאל's hand. Without that cooling, no one from the Jewish people would have survived.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חנא בר ביזנא said in the name of רבי שמעון חסידא: If the coals had not cooled as they passed from the hand of the כרוב to the hand of גבריאל, not a single survivor or escapee would have remained of 'the enemies of Israel'.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא explains the meaning of the change noticed in the previous step. The handoff weakened the punishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because גבריאל received the coals secondhand, they lost some of their heat. That made the destruction less than total. 'The enemies of Israel' is a polite way of saying Israel itself, to avoid speaking of harm to the Jewish people directly.

keyTerms.meaning: The angel גבריאל, the 'man clothed in linen'
'The enemies of Israel'; a polite way of saying Israel itself

steps.confusionAlert: 'The enemies of Israel' does not mean actual enemies. It is a polite way of saying the Jewish people themselves would not have survived.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the change from the command (taking vs. being handed the coals) actually saved the nation. That same change is why גבריאל is punished in the next steps.

phrases.english: Rav Ḥana bar Bizna said
that Rabbi Shimon Ḥasida said:
Had the coals not cooled

phrases.aramaic: מִיָּדוֹ שֶׁל כְּרוּב לְיָדוֹ שֶׁל גַּבְרִיאֵל —
phrases.english: from the hand of the cherub to the hand of Gabriel,
there would not have remained of the enemies of Israel
phrases.notes: A polite way of saying Israel itself

phrases.english: a survivor or an escapee.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חָנָא בַּר בִּיזְנָא אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן חֲסִידָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the meaning of the handoff in the פסוק
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The coals cooled during the handoff, and this is what let the Jewish people survive.

steps.title: גבריאל reports that the mission is done
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a פסוק in which the man clothed in linen reports, 'I have done as You commanded me.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is written: 'And behold, the man clothed in linen, with the scribe's case at his waist, brought back word, saying: I have done as You commanded me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק as a setup for רבי יוחנן's teaching in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: גבריאל claims he did exactly as commanded. But we just saw that he received the coals from the כרוב instead of taking them himself. The report itself will also be criticized.

keyTerms.meaning: The scribe's case (for ink and pen)

phrases.english: And it is written: 'And behold, the man clothed in linen,'
with the scribe's case at his waist,
brought back word, saying:
I have done as You commanded me.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new פסוק to set up the next teaching
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גבריאל reported that he did as commanded.

steps.title: גבריאל is cast out and struck with fire
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says that at that moment גבריאל was removed from behind the פרגוד (the inner heavenly curtain) and struck sixty fiery lashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: At that moment they took גבריאל out from behind the פרגוד and struck him with sixty lashes of fire.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן tells what happened to גבריאל after his report. He was punished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being sent out from behind the פרגוד means losing his place among the closest angels. The reasons for the punishment come in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The heavenly curtain; the inner angels stand behind it

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said: At that moment
they took Gabriel out from behind the curtain,
and struck him sixty lashes of fire.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Describes what happened right after גבריאל's report
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גבריאל was removed from behind the פרגוד and given sixty lashes of fire.

steps.title: Why גבריאל was punished: two charges
steps.stepSummary: The angels give גבריאל two charges. First, if he did the mission, he should have done it exactly as commanded. Second, he should not have given a report about destruction.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: 'If you didn't do it, you didn't do it. If you did it, why didn't you do it the way you were commanded? And besides, once you did it, don't you know the rule that one does not report back about destruction?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the two reasons גבריאל was punished. One is about how he carried out the mission, and one is about his report.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Charge one: he let the כרוב hand him the coals instead of taking them himself, which changed the mission. Charge two: even after a mission of destruction is done, one should not announce its success. That explains why his words 'I have done as You commanded me' were wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: If you did not do it
One does not bring back a report about destruction

steps.whatToRemember: גבריאל did two things wrong. He changed how the mission was carried out (he received the coals instead of taking them), and he reported the destruction. Yet that very change is what saved the Jewish people.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two charges. The first is about how the mission was done. The second (וְעוֹד) is about the report itself, even if the mission had been done perfectly.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: אִי לָא עֲבַדְתְּ — לָא עֲבַדְתְּ,
phrases.english: They said to him: If you didn't do it, you didn't do it;

phrases.aramaic: אִי עֲבַדְתְּ — אַמַּאי לָא עֲבַדְתְּ כִּדְפַקְּדוּךְ?
phrases.english: if you did it, why didn't you do it as you were commanded?
And moreover, once you did it,

phrases.aramaic: לֵית לָךְ אֵין מְשִׁיבִין עַל הַקַּלְקָלָה?
phrases.english: don't you hold that one does not report back about destruction?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: אִי לָא עֲבַדְתְּ — לָא עֲבַדְתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasons for the punishment in the previous step
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גבריאל was punished for changing how the mission was carried out and for reporting on destruction.

steps.title: The angel of Persia replaces גבריאל
steps.stepSummary: After גבריאל is removed, דוביאל, the heavenly prince of Persia, is put in his place and serves for twenty-one days.
steps.simpleTranslation: They brought דוביאל, the angel-prince of the Persians, and set him up in גבריאל's place, and he served for twenty-one days.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues: גבריאל has been removed from his post, so another angel, דוביאל, is put in his place for twenty-one days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Who serves inside matters here. דוביאל is the heavenly representative of Persia, Israel's ruler at that time. So putting him in גבריאל's post means Persia's interests now have influence in heaven.

keyTerms.meaning: The name of the heavenly prince of Persia
A prince or ministering angel appointed over a nation

phrases.english: They brought Dubiel
the prince (angel) of the Persians
and placed him in his (Gabriel's) place,
and he served for twenty-one days.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows what happened after גבריאל was punished and removed (steps 8 to 9).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דוביאל of Persia replaced גבריאל for twenty-one days.

steps.title: A verse in דניאל about the twenty-one days
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that the twenty-one days come from a פסוק in דניאל, where the prince of Persia stood against the speaker for twenty-one days until מיכאל came to help.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what is written: 'The prince of the kingdom of Persia stood against me for twenty-one days, and then מיכאל, one of the chief princes, came to help me, and I stayed there beside the kings of Persia.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the story with a פסוק from ספר דניאל that mentions the prince of Persia and twenty-one days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'הַיְינוּ דִּכְתִיב' means 'this is what the verse means.' It ties the story to the text. The 'prince of Persia' in the פסוק is דוביאל, and the twenty-one days match his time of service.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what is written; this explains the verse
The prince of the kingdom of Persia
The angel מיכאל, protector of Israel

phrases.english: This is what is written:
"But the prince of the kingdom of Persia
stood opposed to me for twenty-one days,
and behold, Michael,
one of the chief princes,
came to help me,
and I remained there
beside the kings of Persia" (Daniel 10:13),

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a verse to support step 10.
steps.raayaObject: That the prince of Persia served (or held power) for twenty-one days

steps.title: Persia is given twenty-one kings and משהיג
steps.stepSummary: Matching the twenty-one days, Persia's angel was given twenty-one kings and the port city of משהיג.
steps.simpleTranslation: They gave him twenty-one kings and the seaport of משהיג.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells us what Persia gained from דוביאל's twenty-one days in power. Persia received twenty-one kings and a seaport.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each day of heavenly power turned into earthly power: one king per day. This shows that what happens in heaven shapes what happens to nations on earth.

phrases.english: They gave him twenty-one kings
and the seaport of Mashhig.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the result of דוביאל's twenty-one days.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Persia received twenty-one kings and the port of משהיג, one king for each day.

steps.title: דוביאל has a tax decree written against Israel and the רבנן
steps.stepSummary: דוביאל asks for a written decree taxing the Jews, and then one taxing the רבנן. Both are written.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: 'Write for me that Israel must pay tax.' They wrote it. 'Write for me that the רבנן must pay tax.' They wrote it.
steps.whatsHappening: דוביאל uses his new power to get the heavenly court to write decrees. One makes the Jews pay tax to Persia, and another makes even the Torah scholars pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two steps here. First comes a tax on all of Israel. Then comes a tax on the רבנן, who were normally exempt. The decrees are written but not yet sealed, and this sets up the next scene.

keyTerms.meaning: Head tax; a tax paid to the government

phrases.english: He said: Write for me
that Israel is subject to the head tax.
They wrote it for him.
Write for me that the Sages are subject to the head tax.
They wrote it for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: דוביאל now uses the power described in steps 10 to 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Decrees taxing Israel and the רבנן were written in heaven, but not yet signed.

steps.title: גבריאל protests with a verse from תהלים
steps.stepSummary: Just as the decree is about to be signed, גבריאל speaks up from outside the curtain and quotes a פסוק from תהלים about those who rise early and stay up late.
steps.simpleTranslation: When they were about to sign it, גבריאל stood outside the curtain and said: 'It is vain for you who rise early and sit up late, eating the bread of toil; so He gives His beloved sleep.'
steps.whatsHappening: At the last moment before signing, גבריאל objects by quoting a פסוק. The גמרא will explain what this פסוק means in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: גבריאל has no post now, so he can only speak from outside. His פסוק hints at the hard life of the Torah scholars and their families. He is arguing that they deserve reward, not a new tax.
steps.confusionAlert: 'מֵאֲחוֹרֵי הַפַּרְגּוֹד' here means גבריאל is standing OUTSIDE the curtain, because he was removed in step 8. He is not inside the inner chamber.

phrases.english: At the time when they wanted to sign,
Gabriel stood from behind the curtain and said:
"It is vain for you who rise up early,
who sit up late,
who eat the bread of toil;
so He gives His beloved sleep" (Psalms 127:2),

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעִידָּנָא דְּבָעוּ לְמִיחְתַּם עָמַד גַּבְרִיאֵל מֵאֲחוֹרֵי הַפַּרְגּוֹד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: גבריאל responds to the decree written in step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גבריאל protests the tax on the רבנן by quoting תהלים קכז:ב.

steps.title: What does 'He gives His beloved sleep' mean
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pauses the story to ask what the end of גבריאל's פסוק means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is meant by 'so He gives His beloved sleep'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question about the פסוק. This sets up רבי יצחק's explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'He gives His beloved sleep' are unclear. Who loses sleep, and why does that matter? Unless we understand this, we cannot see why גבריאל's פסוק is an argument against the tax.

phrases.english: What is "so He gives His beloved sleep"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what the פסוק quoted in step 14 means.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of 'כֵּן יִתֵּן לִידִידוֹ שֵׁנָא'

steps.title: רבי יצחק: the wives of תלמידי חכמים
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק explains that the פסוק refers to the wives of תלמידי חכמים. They give up sleep in this world and earn עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק said: These are the wives of Torah scholars, who lose sleep in this world and earn the World to Come.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק answers the question. The 'beloved' who lose sleep are the wives of Torah scholars, who stay up waiting for their husbands to come home from learning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now גבריאל's argument makes sense. These families already give up so much for Torah. Is a new tax their reward? This is the heart of his defense of the רבנן.

keyTerms.meaning: And merit the World to Come

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a famous source praising the wives of תלמידי חכמים. Their sacrifice is counted as a real merit and shares in the Torah learning.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak said:
These are the wives of Torah scholars
who give up sleep in this world
and merit the World to Come,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: אֵלּוּ נְשׁוֹתֵיהֶן שֶׁל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The 'beloved' are the wives of תלמידי חכמים, who give up sleep and earn עולם הבא.

steps.title: No one listens to גבריאל
steps.stepSummary: The heavenly court ignores גבריאל's protest.
steps.simpleTranslation: But they paid no attention to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The story picks up again. גבריאל's first argument, for the scholars and their wives, is ignored.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His first try fails. This sets up his second argument in the next step, where he praises דניאל.

phrases.english: And they paid no attention to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tells us how the court reacted to גבריאל's protest (step 14).

steps.title: גבריאל argues that דניאל outweighs all the wise men of the nations
steps.stepSummary: גבריאל tries again. He says that דניאל alone would outweigh all the wise men of the nations on a scale.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said before Him: 'Master of the World! If all the wise men of the nations were on one side of a scale, and דניאל, the beloved man, on the other side, would he not outweigh them all?'
steps.whatsHappening: גבריאל makes a second argument, speaking straight to הקב"ה. He praises the merit of דניאל, a great Jewish sage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His first argument was about the burden on scholars. This one is about the great worth of Israel's wise men. One Jewish sage is worth more than all the wisdom of the nations, so Israel should not be put under them.

keyTerms.meaning: Beloved (precious) man, a title of דניאל

phrases.english: He said before Him: Master of the World!

phrases.aramaic: אִם יִהְיוּ כׇּל חַכְמֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם
phrases.english: If all the wise men of the nations of the world were
on one pan of a scale,
and Daniel, the beloved man, on the second pan,
would he not be found to outweigh them all?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: גבריאל's second try after the first was ignored.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דניאל alone outweighs all the wise men of the nations.

steps.title: God asks who is defending His children, and calls גבריאל in
steps.stepSummary: הקב"ה asks who is speaking up for His children. The angels say it is גבריאל, and הקב"ה says: let him come.
steps.simpleTranslation: הקב"ה said: 'Who is this who speaks in defense of My children?' They said: 'Master of the World, it is גבריאל.' He said to them: 'Let him come.'
steps.whatsHappening: This time הקב"ה responds. He asks who is defending Israel and invites גבריאל to come in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second argument works. By praising דניאל, גבריאל spoke in favor of Israel, and that earns him a hearing. Notice that הקב"ה calls Israel 'My children.'

keyTerms.meaning: Speaks in someone's defense, argues for their merit

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said:

phrases.aramaic: מִי הוּא זֶה שֶׁמְּלַמֵּד זְכוּת עַל בָּנַי?
phrases.english: Who is this who defends My children?

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לְפָנָיו: רִבּוֹנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, גַּבְרִיאֵל.
phrases.english: They said before Him: Master of the World, it is Gabriel.
He said to them: Let him come.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי הוּא זֶה שֶׁמְּלַמֵּד זְכוּת עַל בָּנַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: הקב"ה responds to גבריאל's argument about דניאל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Because גבריאל defended Israel, הקב"ה allowed him to return.

steps.title: Verse: 'And I have come because of your words'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports this with a פסוק from דניאל: 'And I have come because of your words.'
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'And I have come because of your words.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק to show that גבריאל came back because of דניאל's words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק, the angel tells דניאל 'I have come because of your words.' The גמרא reads it like this: גבריאל was let back in because of דניאל, whose merit he had mentioned.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said (introduces a verse)

phrases.english: As it is said: "And I have come because of your words" (Daniel 10:12).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a verse to support step 19.
steps.raayaObject: That גבריאל came back in because of דניאל

steps.title: גבריאל is brought back inside
steps.stepSummary: הקב"ה tells the angels to bring גבריאל in, and they do.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: 'Let him enter.' They brought him in.
steps.whatsHappening: גבריאל is officially let back inside the curtain. Now he can act against the decree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His return to the inside undoes his removal from step 8. This sets up the struggle over the decree in the next step.

phrases.english: He said to them: Let him enter.
They brought him in.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Carries out הקב"ה's 'let him come' from step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גבריאל was brought back inside the curtain.

steps.title: דוביאל swallows the decree
steps.stepSummary: גבריאל finds דוביאל holding the decree. When he tries to take it away, דוביאל swallows it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He came and found דוביאל holding his letter in his hand. He tried to snatch it from him, but he swallowed it.
steps.whatsHappening: Back inside, גבריאל tries to grab the tax decree from דוביאל. דוביאל swallows it so it cannot be taken.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the climax of the struggle. Destroying the decree would cancel it, but swallowing it leaves things unclear. The גמרא will next ask how far the decree had already gone.

phrases.english: He came and found Dubiel
holding his letter in his hand,
he wanted to snatch it from him,
he (Dubiel) swallowed it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: גבריאל, now back inside, goes after the decree from step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דוביאל swallowed the decree to keep גבריאל from taking it.

steps.title: First version: the decree was written but not signed
steps.stepSummary: One opinion says the decree had been written but was never signed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: it had been written, but it had not been signed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the first of two versions about the state of the decree when it was swallowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, the decree was never finished, because it was never signed. So it never fully took effect.

phrases.english: Some say:
it was written,
but it was not signed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Describes the state of the decree that was swallowed in step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The decree was written but not signed.

steps.title: Second version: it was signed, but swallowing erased it
steps.stepSummary: A second opinion says the decree was signed too, but the signature was rubbed out when דוביאל swallowed it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Others say: it was signed too, but when he swallowed it, it was erased.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the second version. The decree was fully signed, but it got smudged when it was swallowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both versions reach the same result: the decree is incomplete. The first says it was never signed. The second says the signature was ruined. Either way, it is only partly valid.

phrases.english: Some say:
it was even signed as well,
but when he swallowed it, it was erased from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: אַף מִיחְתָּם נָמֵי הֲוָה חֲתִימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version that differs from step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The decree was signed, but the signature was erased by the swallowing.

steps.title: Why some in Persia pay tax and some do not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that this is why, under Persian rule, some people pay the head tax and some do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is why, in the kingdom of Persia, there are some who pay the head tax and some who do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses the half-finished decree to explain a fact of real life: in Persia, the tax was paid by some and not by others.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The decree was only partly valid, so it only partly took effect. This ties the heavenly story to the uneven tax situation that people actually saw in Persia.
steps.whatToRemember: The tax decree on Israel and the רבנן was never fully completed. It was either unsigned or its signature was erased, so in Persia some paid the tax and some did not.

phrases.english: This is why in the kingdom of Persia
there are those who pay the head tax
and there are those who do not pay the head tax.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a real-world result from the half-finished decree in steps 23 to 24.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The incomplete decree explains why only some people in Persia paid the head tax.

steps.title: Greece rises and גבריאל cries out unheard
steps.stepSummary: Quoting דניאל, 'as I leave, the prince of Greece comes,' the גמרא says גבריאל cried out again and again, but no one paid attention.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'As I go out, behold, the prince of Greece comes.' He cried out and cried out, but there was no one who paid attention to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves to the next empire, Greece. גבריאל protests strongly against Greece ruling over Israel, but this time he is not heard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ending is the opposite of his success with Persia. Against Greece, his cries change nothing. It hints that the rule of Greece over Israel had already been decided.

phrases.english: "And as I go out,
behold, the prince of Greece comes" (Daniel 10:20),
he cried out and cried out,
and there was no one who paid attention to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from Persia to the next empire, Greece, and contrasts גבריאל's earlier partial success.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גבריאל protested Greek rule over Israel, but no one listened.

steps.title: Another way to find that bathing counts as affliction
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to its main topic. It offers a new way to show that holding back from רחיצה is called עינוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you prefer, say: the idea that bathing is called 'affliction', where do we learn it from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the story about גבריאל and goes back to the question of where we learn that not bathing is עינוי. This line sets up a new search for a source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא brought a source from דניאל, and that source led into the long story. Now, with 'ואי בעית אימא', it tries a completely different source for the same law.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Or if you prefer, say', which introduces another explanation or another source
Affliction, the עינוי the תורה commands on יום כיפור
From where do we know this?

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
that bathing is called affliction, from where do we know it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא: רְחִיצָה דְּאִיקְּרִי עִנּוּי מְנָא לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the aggadah of steps 1-26 and goes back to the halachic question that came before it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק showing that not bathing is called עינוי.

steps.title: Proof from אביתר and דוד being 'weary'
steps.stepSummary: שלמה tells אביתר that he suffered along with דוד. Elsewhere, דוד's people are described as hungry, weary, and thirsty. 'Weary' must mean from not bathing.
steps.simpleTranslation: From here, as it is written: 'And to אביתר the כהן the king said: Go to ענתות, to your fields, for you deserve death. But today I will not put you to death, because you carried the ארון of God before דוד my father, and because you were afflicted in everything my father was afflicted.' And it is written about דוד: 'For they said, the people are hungry, weary, and thirsty in the wilderness.' Hungry means from lack of bread, thirsty means from lack of water. Weary from what? Is it not from lack of bathing?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings two פסוקים together. דוד's suffering is called 'עינוי', and that suffering included being hungry, thirsty, and weary. Since hungry and thirsty are already explained, 'weary' must mean from not bathing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק calls what דוד went through 'התענה', which is the language of עינוי. The second פסוק spells out what that suffering was: hungry, weary, thirsty. Hungry means no food and thirsty means no drink, so the leftover word 'עיף' is read as no bathing. That would make not bathing a kind of עינוי.

keyTerms.meaning: אביתר the כהן, who stayed with דוד during his hard times
You were afflicted; the same root as עינוי
Is it not? This introduces the suggested answer

phrases.english: From here, as it is written:
"And to Ebiathar the priest the king said:
Go to Anatoth, to your fields,
for you deserve death;
but on this day I will not put you to death,
because you carried the Ark of God
before David my father,
and because you were afflicted in all
that my father was afflicted."
And it is written about David:
"For they said, the people are
hungry, weary, and thirsty in the wilderness."
Hungry is from bread, and thirsty is from water;
weary is from what? Is it not from bathing?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 27 with a proposed source.
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלכים א ב:כו together with שמואל ב יז:כט, reading 'עיף' as 'from not bathing'.

steps.title: Maybe 'weary' means from going without shoes
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed away. 'Weary' could just as well mean tired from walking without shoes.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps it means weary from lack of wearing shoes?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that 'weary' does not have to mean from not bathing. It could mean tired from walking barefoot, so the proof falls apart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof worked only if 'עיף' could mean nothing except not bathing. Going barefoot also makes a person weary, so the פסוק does not prove anything about רחיצה.

keyTerms.meaning: But perhaps; this introduces another possible reading

phrases.english: But perhaps it is from wearing shoes?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 28.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from אביתר and דוד.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: 'עיף' could mean tired from walking barefoot, not from not bathing.

steps.title: רבי יצחק's proof: cold water on a weary soul
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק brings a new proof from משלי. Cold water helps a 'weary soul', which shows that 'weary' is connected to not having water on the body.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי יצחק said: from here: 'Like cold water on a weary soul.'
steps.whatsHappening: Since the first proof failed, רבי יצחק brings a new פסוק. It ties being 'weary' to needing cold water, which suggests bathing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the cure for being 'עיפה' is cold water. That shows 'weary' describes someone who needs water, meaning someone who has not bathed. So not bathing is the weariness that counts as עינוי.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; this drops the earlier idea and brings a new one

phrases.english: Rather, Rabbi Yitzchak said: from here:
"Like cold water on a weary soul."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the proof that was rejected in step 29.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משלי כה:כה, 'מים קרים על נפש עיפה'.

steps.title: Maybe the cold water is for drinking
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יצחק: maybe the cold water helps someone who is weary from thirst.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps it means weary from not drinking?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks if the cold water in the פסוק is for drinking, not for washing. If so, the פסוק is about thirst and not about bathing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Cold water helps a thirsty person just as much as an unwashed one. If the פסוק means drinking, it says nothing about רחיצה.

phrases.english: But perhaps it is from drinking?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי יצחק's proof.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יצחק's reading of משלי כה:כה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Cold water could be meant for drinking, which would make the פסוק about thirst.

steps.title: The word 'on' shows it means washing
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says the water is 'על' (on) the soul, not 'ב' (in) it. Water put on a person means washing, not drinking.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it written 'in a weary soul'? It is written 'on a weary soul'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers from the exact wording. Water 'on' a person is washing, while water 'in' a person would be drinking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Drinking puts water inside the body, so the פסוק would have said 'בנפש'. Because it says 'על נפש', the water goes on the outside of the body, which is bathing. So רבי יצחק's proof stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it written...? This points out what the פסוק does not say

steps.whatToRemember: The source that not bathing is עינוי is 'מים קרים על נפש עיפה'. The word 'על' (on) shows the water is for washing, not drinking.

phrases.english: Is it written "in a weary soul"?
"On a weary soul" is written.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Exact reading of the פסוק's wording (על versus ב).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The cold water might be for drinking.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'על' means the water is on the body, which is bathing, so the proof holds.

steps.title: Where do we learn that going without shoes is affliction?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא moves on to the next item in the משנה and asks for the source for נעילת הסנדל.
steps.simpleTranslation: And wearing shoes, from where do we know it is included?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next item on the משנה's list. It asks for a source that holding back from wearing shoes counts as עינוי, which sets up a new search.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With bathing proven, the גמרא now needs a source for the ban on wearing shoes. The method stays the same: find a פסוק where going barefoot is part of suffering.

keyTerms.meaning: And wearing shoes, the next item in the משנה

phrases.english: And wearing shoes, from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from bathing to the next item in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source that holding back from wearing shoes counts as עינוי.

steps.title: Proof from דוד walking barefoot up the Mount of Olives
steps.stepSummary: While fleeing אבשלום, דוד went up הר הזיתים crying, with his head covered and barefoot. 'Barefoot' means without shoes, as part of his suffering.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And דוד went up the ascent of הר הזיתים, going up and weeping, with his head covered, and walking barefoot.' Barefoot from what? Is it not from wearing shoes?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק where דוד, in a time of suffering, walked barefoot. It suggests that 'barefoot' means without shoes, so going without shoes is a form of suffering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דוד was in deep distress, crying with his head covered. The פסוק adds that he was barefoot, so going without shoes appears as part of that affliction. That would make holding back from shoes a kind of עינוי.

keyTerms.meaning: The ascent of הר הזיתים (the Mount of Olives)

phrases.english: As it is written: "And David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives,
going up and weeping,
with his head covered,
(and walking) barefoot."
Barefoot from what? Is it not from wearing shoes?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 33 with a proposed source.
steps.raayaObject: Holding back from wearing shoes counts as עינוי.

steps.title: Maybe 'barefoot' means without his horse and whip
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed away. For a king, 'barefoot' could mean walking without his horse and whip, even while wearing shoes.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps it means without a horse and a whip.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says 'barefoot' here may not be literal. A king who walks instead of riding his horse is called 'barefoot' even if he has shoes on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a king, riding with a horse and whip was normal and showed his honor. Walking without them could be called being 'barefoot'. So the פסוק does not prove that דוד took off his shoes.

phrases.english: But perhaps it is from a horse and a whip.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 34.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from דוד on הר הזיתים.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: 'יחף' may mean without his royal horse and whip, not without shoes.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק's proof from ישעיהו
steps.stepSummary: ה׳ told ישעיהו to take off his sackcloth and his shoe, and he walked 'naked and barefoot'. Here 'barefoot' clearly comes right after an order to remove his shoe.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב נחמן בר יצחק said: from here: 'Go and loosen the sackcloth from your loins, and take your shoe off your foot.' And it is written: 'And he did so, walking naked and barefoot.' Barefoot from what? Is it not from wearing shoes?
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק brings a new פסוק. In it, ישעיהו is told to take off his shoes and then walks 'barefoot' as a sign of suffering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This פסוק is stronger because the order to 'remove your shoe' comes right before the word 'barefoot'. So 'יחף' here seems to really mean without shoes, and it is part of a picture of suffering. That would show that going without shoes is a kind of עינוי.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק, מֵהָכָא:
phrases.english: Rather, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: from here:
"Go and loosen the sackcloth from your loins,
and remove your shoe from your foot,"
and it is written: "And he did so,
walking naked and barefoot."
Barefoot from what? Is it not from wearing shoes?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק, מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the proof that was rejected in step 35.
steps.raayaObject: Holding back from wearing shoes counts as עינוי.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ישעיהו כ:ב, the order to remove his shoe followed by walking 'ערום ויחף'.

steps.title: Maybe ישעיהו just wore patched shoes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן בר יצחק: 'naked' cannot mean really naked, only wearing torn clothes. In the same way, 'barefoot' may just mean wearing patched shoes.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say it means with patched shoes! For if you do not say so, does 'naked' mean truly naked? Rather, it means in worn-out clothes. Here too, it means in patched shoes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא argues that 'barefoot' may not be literal. The same פסוק says 'naked', and no one thinks a נביא walked around truly naked. This challenge is accepted: in the next step רב נחמן בר יצחק drops this proof and brings a different verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'ערום' must mean wearing shabby clothes, not literally naked. Since 'יחף' sits right next to it, it may also be non-literal and mean worn, patched shoes. If so, ישעיהו was still wearing shoes, and the proof that going shoeless is עינוי is weakened.

keyTerms.meaning: Here too; this applies the same reasoning to the case at hand

steps.confusionAlert: 'עָרוֹם מַמָּשׁ' is not a statement that ישעיהו was really naked. It is a rhetorical question: 'Does it mean truly naked?' The obvious answer is no, and that answer is what powers the challenge.

phrases.english: But say it was with patched shoes?
For if you do not say so,
"naked": does it mean actually naked?
Rather, it means in worn-out clothes;
here too, it means in patched shoes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof of step 36.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן בר יצחק's reading of 'יחף' in ישעיהו.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'ערום' in the same פסוק is not literal and means shabby clothes. So 'יחף' may also be non-literal and mean patched shoes, not no shoes at all.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: 'ערום' in the same פסוק is not literal (worn-out clothes), so 'יחף' may also be non-literal and mean patched shoes, not no shoes at all.

steps.title: A new proof from ירמיהו that being barefoot is suffering
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק drops his earlier proof and brings a verse from ירמיהו. The verse treats going barefoot as a punishment, so it is a real form of suffering.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב נחמן בר יצחק said the source is from here: 'Keep your foot from going barefoot, and your throat from thirst.' This means: keep yourself away from sin, so that your foot will not end up barefoot. Keep your tongue away from idle talk, so that your throat will not end up thirsty.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the ישעיהו proof was weakened, רב נחמן בר יצחק replaces it with a different verse. He explains that ירמיהו warns the people that sin will lead to being barefoot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse describes being barefoot as a punishment that comes from sin, as when people are driven into exile. Something given as a punishment must be real suffering. So being barefoot is a type of עינוי, and wearing shoes is what we hold back from on יום כיפור. This verse does not have the weakness of the earlier proofs, because here 'barefoot' is clearly meant as hardship.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. It signals that the earlier proof is dropped and a new one is coming.
From here, meaning from this verse
Idle talk, empty or useless words

steps.whatToRemember: The final source for not wearing shoes on יום כיפור is ירמיהו's warning. Being barefoot is a punishment, so it counts as suffering (עינוי).
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the proof that holds up for counting נעילת הסנדל among the five afflictions of יום כיפור.

steps.title: Where do we learn that holding back from marital relations is called suffering?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא moves to the next affliction in the משנה, תשמיש המטה. It asks for the source that holding back from it counts as עינוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Marital relations, which is called 'affliction' — from where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new item from the משנה's list. It is setting up the next move by asking for a verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows the same pattern used for washing, anointing, and shoes: for each affliction, the גמרא looks for a verse where that kind of holding back is called עינוי. The answer comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know this?

steps.title: לבן's warning to יעקב: 'if you afflict my daughters'
steps.stepSummary: The answer comes from לבן's words to יעקב, which use the word 'afflict' right next to 'taking other wives.' This shows that afflicting a wife here means holding back marital relations.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'If you afflict my daughters, and if you take other wives…'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a verse from בראשית, where לבן warns יעקב how to treat his daughters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'if you afflict my daughters' stands right next to 'if you take other wives.' Read together, the 'affliction' means holding back marital relations from them. So holding back from תשמיש המטה is called עינוי.
steps.confusionAlert: The verse does not say 'relations' openly. The proof comes from reading 'afflict' together with the words right next to it, 'taking other wives.'

phrases.english: As it is written:

phrases.notes: Because these words come right next to 'afflict,' the affliction is understood as holding back marital relations.
